title: The years in the forests
hook: a price is set on Sikh heads and the Khalsa survives in jungles and deserts

segments.voice: Yesterday, Banda's end in Delhi: true to the end. With their leader gone, how did the Sikhs go on?

The thick scrub forest of central Punjab, after dark. No roads, no lamps. A few riders move through it quietly, horses tied in the undergrowth, supper cooking on a low fire that won't be seen from the plain. Back in the towns, a notice has gone up: a reward for every Sikh brought in, alive or dead. These riders have left everything. And around the fire, surprisingly, somebody is laughing.
screen: `SCRUB FOREST, AFTER DARK.` → `A REWARD FOR EVERY SIKH.` → `AROUND THE FIRE, LAUGHTER.`

segments.voice: After 1716, the Mughal governors of Punjab set out to finish the Khalsa. For long stretches over the next decades, a price was put on Sikh heads, and people were rewarded for turning them in. Being recognized as a Sikh, with uncut hair and a turban, could cost you your life. Some Sikhs cut their hair and stayed in the villages. Many of the Khalsa went where soldiers couldn't easily follow: the scrub jungles of Punjab, the foothills of the Himalaya, the edges of the Rajasthan desert. They moved in small bands, lived on what they could find or what villagers quietly gave them, and struck back when they could. And they kept coming home in secret. Tradition says riders would slip into Amritsar by night to bathe in the pool at the Harmandir, and be gone before morning. What kept them going? Faith, first: daily prayers said in the open air, the Guru Granth Sahib honored even in a camp. And a fierce, stubborn humor. The Khalsa built up its own playful way of talking. One rider on his own might call himself an army. Plain rough food got grand names. Tradition credits Guru Gobind Singh with the saying that one Sikh would stand against sava lakh, a hundred and twenty-five thousand, and the riders took it at its word, with a grin. In 1733 the government in Lahore, unable to finish them, offered the Khalsa a truce, land and the title of Nawab. The Khalsa gave the title to Kapur Singh, who was fanning the sangat when the offer came. The truce didn't last, and harder years were coming. But a small, hunted people, living under the stars for decades, wasn't crushed. They survived.
screen: `A PRICE ON SIKH HEADS.` · `JUNGLES, HILLS AND DESERTS.` · `SECRET NIGHTS AT THE POOL.` · `ONE RIDER IS SAVA LAKH.` · then, large: `THEY SURVIVED.`

segments.voice: Look around the room you're in, the walls, the roof, the door you can lock, and notice one thing that keeps you safe and warm. Then think of the riders in the scrub, and of anyone tonight with no safe place to sleep, and let gratitude for your shelter rise, without guilt. If you pray, you can hold them in it.
Sava lakh. One and a quarter lakh, 125,000, the number one Sikh is said to stand against; the hunted Khalsa took it at its word, with a grin, and survived.
Your line: they survived. Hunted for decades, and still laughing around the fire. Until tomorrow, then.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember the eighteenth-century years of persecution in Ardas and in stories told at gurdwaras; the Khalsa's playful coded speech from that time, sometimes called Khalsa bole, is still used by Nihangs.

what it means: for decades, with a price on their heads, the Khalsa lived in jungles, hills and deserts, kept its faith and humor, and was never crushed.
what a scholar hears: persecution under governors such as Zakariya Khan (1726–45); the Khalsa's in-group speech (Khalsa or Nihang bole) likely took shape in these years.

chat.says: How did the Sikhs survive with a price on their heads for years?
options: Small bands lived in the forests, kept their prayers, and held onto a stubborn humor.
Every one of them cut their hair and blended into the towns until it passed.
They left Punjab for good and built new lives in faraway kingdoms.
chat.meaning: Hunted Khalsa bands lived in scrub and hills, held to daily prayer, and joked their way through. One rider could be sava lakh.
